lesson.title: You Carry Mine, I'll Carry Yours: How Peering Works
lesson.summary: Peering is a settlement free agreement between two networks to exchange traffic destined for each other's own customers directly, without either side paying the other.
lesson.body:
Peering is the relationship that makes tier 1 status possible, and it also happens constantly at smaller scales throughout the rest of the internet, so it deserves its own close look. Two networks peer when they agree to interconnect and exchange traffic directly with each other, and, crucially, agree to do so without either side paying the other, on the reasoning that the value each side gets from the arrangement is roughly balanced: each network gets a shorter, often faster and cheaper path to reach the other's customers than it would get by routing that traffic through a paid transit provider instead.

The scope of what gets carried over a peering connection is narrower than it might first sound, and this is where the underlying BGP policy machinery, and interdomain routing's business awareness generally, becomes visible as a concrete rule. A network that peers with another does not, by default, agree to carry that peer's traffic onward to some third network, only to and from its own customers. In BGP terms, a network typically only advertises its own customer routes to a peer, and only accepts and forwards a peer's customer routes to its own customers, not out to its other peers or providers. This is why peering is considered a bounded, reciprocal arrangement rather than open ended transit: an autonomous system does not get free unlimited access to everywhere its peer can reach, only to the peer itself and the peer's own customers.

Peering can happen in two practical forms. Private peering is a direct physical link installed between two networks specifically to carry traffic between them. Public peering happens at an internet exchange point, a shared facility where many networks connect to a common switching fabric and can establish peering sessions with several other participants over that single connection, which is considerably more efficient than each pair of networks running its own dedicated link, especially once many networks want to peer with each other in the same city or region. Whether the reasons two networks decide to peer are driven by reduced cost, better performance, or simple mutual convenience, the underlying logic is always the same trade: comparable amounts of traffic and value flow in each direction, so neither side asks the other to pay.
